prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Apollo 13 left Kennedy Space Center on April 11, 1970, carrying James Lovell, Fred Haise and Jack Swigert toward what was meant to be the third landing on the Moon, and Swigert was aboard only because the original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles by a colleague a few days earlier and flight surgeons had grounded him. Lovell was the most experienced spacefarer of the group, a veteran of Gemini and of Apollo 8's loop around the Moon, while Haise was a rookie assigned to pilot the lunar module and Swigert had trained for the mission for only a matter of days. The launch was mostly smooth apart from a violent vibration in the Saturn V's second stage that shut its center engine down early, and the remaining engines burned longer to make up the difference, so that the crew reached orbit and then set out for the Moon on schedule, christening their command module Odyssey and their lunar module Aquarius.

For two days the flight was so uneventful that television networks declined to carry the crew's broadcast on the evening of April 13, and the astronauts used the transmission to show viewers around their cabin, with Lovell remarking that the ship was a comfortable home. Shortly afterward, at about fifty-five hours and fifty-five minutes into the mission and roughly 200,000 miles from Earth, Mission Control asked Swigert to switch on the fans that stirred the supercritical oxygen and hydrogen stored in the service module's tanks, a routine step that kept the cryogenic fluids from stratifying and gave the gauges accurate readings. Within a minute or two a bang shook the spacecraft, the lights flickered, and Swigert said that they had a problem, a line Lovell repeated a moment later for the benefit of the controllers in Houston who had already begun to see their telemetry fall apart.

What had happened was that oxygen tank number two had ruptured. The tank had been damaged on the ground before the mission, when it was accidentally dropped a couple of inches during removal from a previous spacecraft, and then during a countdown test at the Cape technicians had been unable to drain it in the normal way and had instead boiled off the oxygen with the internal heaters, which had been designed for the spacecraft's 28-volt supply but were exposed to 65 volts from ground equipment, welding their thermostat switches shut and baking the Teflon insulation on the wiring inside. When Swigert threw the fan switch, a spark from that bared wiring ignited the insulation in the pure oxygen, pressure climbed until the tank burst, and the blast blew a whole panel off the side of the service module and left the neighbouring oxygen tank leaking its contents into space. The three fuel cells that made the ship's electricity and water depended on that oxygen, so over the next couple of hours the power drained away, the command module's remaining battery life was reserved for the final descent, and it became clear that Odyssey was dying.

The only lifeboat available was Aquarius, which was built to carry two men for a day and a half on the lunar surface and now had to sustain three men for about four days, so the crew shut down the command module, climbed through the tunnel with the lunar module's own supplies of power, oxygen and water, and began to live in a craft that was never meant to be a home. In Houston the flight director Gene Kranz and his relief shifts of controllers abandoned any idea of landing and concentrated on the question of how to return, and because the spacecraft had earlier been placed on a trajectory that would miss the Earth had it simply swung around the Moon, they used the lunar module's descent engine, which had been designed to land on the Moon, to fire the ship back onto a path that would bring it home. A second burn a few hours after passing the far side of the Moon, in which the crew flew farther from Earth than any humans had gone before, at nearly 250,000 miles, sped up the return and moved the splashdown point into the Pacific where recovery ships were waiting, though that left the crew a cold and thirsty three days to endure.

The trip home was punishing in ways that tested the men more than the engineers had anticipated, because Aquarius made very little electricity and the crew turned off almost everything to save it, which allowed the cabin to chill to near freezing, with condensation running down the walls and the men sleeping poorly in their light flight suits while Haise developed a fever from a urinary infection, and the water ration was cut to a few ounces each per day, so that all three arrived home dehydrated, with Lovell having lost about fourteen pounds. A more urgent hazard came when the lunar module's lithium hydroxide canisters, which scrubbed carbon dioxide from the air, began to fill up, and the only spare canisters aboard belonged to the command module and were square, so that they did not fit the round receptacles in the lunar module's system. Engineers on the ground gathered the same material the crew had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a spacesuit hose and a roll of duct tape, built an adapter from them, and read the instructions up to the astronauts, who assembled a copy and watched the carbon dioxide level fall.

Mattingly, who had been spared the measles after all, spent long hours in a simulator working out a procedure to start the command module again with the tiny amount of power that remained in its batteries, since nobody had ever powered it up from scratch in flight and the margin was thin enough that any wasted amperage mattered. The ground team wrote the checklist and Mattingly's final version was read up to the crew, and as the ship approached Earth the men also had to correct their course by hand with a burn of the lunar module's engine, aligning the craft by eye using the line between night and day on the Earth, because the guidance platform had been turned off and could not be trusted to find its bearings in time. Shortly before reentry they separated the service module, and when it drifted away they saw for the first time how much of it was ruined, with an entire side torn open and equipment trailing from the gap, which Lovell described to Houston and which finally explained the scale of the disaster.

They then climbed back into Odyssey, which was cold and wet inside but which came to life as the ground had promised, and they jettisoned the lunar module that had saved them, watching it fall away before they prepared for the descent. Reentry brought a final anxiety, because communications blackout from the heat of the atmosphere normally lasts about three minutes and the delay stretched on beyond that, with controllers in Houston silent and watching the clock until, a little more than a minute late, Swigert's voice came through, and soon afterward the parachutes opened and the capsule dropped into the South Pacific on April 17, 1970, near the recovery ship Iwo Jima, almost six days after launch. The crew were weary and unshaven but in sound condition, and Haise recovered from his infection within days.

A review board led by Edgar Cortright found that the accident resulted from the combination of damaged equipment, a thermostat design that had never been updated for the higher voltage, and test procedures that had not caught the overheating, and NASA redesigned the oxygen tanks and removed the wiring that had burned before flying again, with the Apollo programme proceeding to land on the Moon on four further missions. Apollo 13 never reached the lunar surface and none of its goals were met, but it has been remembered as a successful failure because a team of people on the ground and in space improvised solutions to a series of problems that nobody had planned for and brought three men home alive, and it remains one of the clearest demonstrations of what careful training, plain ingenuity and trust between a crew and its controllers can accomplish when the plan has fallen apart.
